subject: Expected argument
assertion: Borrower lacks standing to challenge the assignment; 'show me the note' is universally rejected in Georgia
verification_method: verified as a correct statement of Georgia law
verified_detail: Ames v. JP Morgan Chase Bank, N.A., 298 Ga. 732 (2016) (Nahmias, J.) holds the Ameses lack standing to challenge the assignment of their security deed, affirming Montgomery and Jurden. It cites Haynes v. McCalla Raymer, LLC, 793 F.3d 1246, 1252-53 (11th Cir. 2015) as 'holding that debtors lacked standing to challenge an assignment using OCGA 44-14-162(b) on the ground that the assignment was not properly attested.'
what_it_supports: That this argument will be made and that it is well supported
what_it_does_not_establish: Nothing favourable. This is adverse authority and it is strong.
notes: CITATOR-LIMITED MEDIUM. Any count depending on the validity of an assignment must be treated as facing this head-on.

subject: Counter-move as drafted
assertion: Plead the assignment VOID (not voidable) and cite Ames at 741 as reserving that attack
verification_method: read the Ames opinion full text and searched every occurrence of 'void'
verified_detail: Every use of 'void' in Ames is in FOOTNOTE 8, which surveys OTHER jurisdictions. Its text aligns Georgia with the stricter line: 'some courts have indicated-consistent with our conclusion-that plaintiff debtors ALWAYS lack standing to challenge an assignment when they have failed to prove an injury from the assignment', while 'others have held or suggested that there is debtor standing to challenge an assignment that is truly void'. The void line is described as the view of OTHER courts, expressly contrasted with the Georgia court's own conclusion.
what_it_supports: Nothing. The reservation the playbook relies on is not in the opinion.
what_it_does_not_establish: That Georgia recognises a void-assignment exception to borrower standing
notes: CON-012. PHASE 5 UPDATE - THE DEFECT DID NOT REACH THE PLEADING. SRC-021, the 16-count amended complaint, contains ZERO occurrences of 'Racette', 'Fannie', 'REMIC' or '2024-91', and pleads no void-ab-initio assignment attack. Its P3 was drafted AROUND Ames, not into it. A narrower residual defect survives and is recorded at OC-012. The QuickRef's advice was not followed, which materially lowers the Rule 11 exposure recorded before this check was run.

subject: Recovered value
assertion: Racette is live authority for a DIFFERENT theory this matter may actually have
verification_method: read the Racette opinion full text
verified_detail: Racette reversed dismissal of wrongful-foreclosure, breach-of-contract and emotional-distress claims where the published advertisements referenced a senior lien at a deed book and page that concerned a different property and different borrowers, and where the borrower gave actual notice of the error on the courthouse steps. The court held it could not determine at the motion-to-dismiss stage whether a bidder could have resolved the uncertainty from county records.
what_it_supports: A defective-advertisement theory surviving a motion to dismiss, with emotional-distress damages, where the foreclosing party had actual notice of the defect
what_it_does_not_establish: That this matter has such a defect - no published advertisement has been obtained here
notes: Ties to GAP-007, now promoted to priority 1. Haynes at 1253-54 (CV-026) opens a SECOND theory on the same documents: an O.C.G.A. 44-14-162.2 claim that the foreclosure notice misidentified the entity with full modification authority. Both theories need the notices and neither depends on ownership. Haynes also states what defeats the second one: causation. The defect, not the default, must have caused the harm.

subject: Recovered value
assertion: O.C.G.A. 44-14-162(b) recorded-chain theory as the playbook frames it is foreclosed by authority Ames itself cites
verification_method: read Ames footnote 7 and its citation to Haynes
verified_detail: Haynes read in full (CV-024, CV-025). It forecloses the recorded-chain standing theory on TWO independent grounds: borrowers lack standing to attack an assignment they are not party to, even for a patent attestation defect (at 1253); and O.C.G.A. 44-14-162(b) requires only that the instrument be FILED before sale, saying 'nothing of when (or even if) the deed must actually be recorded' (at 1252).
what_it_does_not_establish: That no 44-14-162 theory survives. Haynes itself reached a 44-14-162.2 NOTICE claim on the merits and rejected it on causation, not on standing - see CV-026. Duke Galish's open question about whether a 44-14-162(b) failure renders the SALE void or voidable is also untouched by Haynes.
notes: PHASE 5: read in full, superseding the parenthetical at CV-020. The playbook's Insert #6 is foreclosed twice over. The door Haynes leaves open is 44-14-162.2, not 44-14-162(b).

subject: Residual pleading defect
assertion: SRC-021 P3 states the pleaded theories 'fall within the carveouts recognized in Ames or attack the enforceability of the underlying obligation independent of any assignment'
verification_method: read Ames in full and searched every occurrence of 'void'
verified_detail: The second branch of that disjunctive is sound and is what Counts X and XI actually do. The FIRST branch is not: Ames recognises no carveouts. Footnote 8 describes carveouts recognised in OTHER jurisdictions and expressly aligns Georgia against them; footnote 7 cites Haynes, which forecloses the nearest candidate. P3 also pincites '738-41 & nn.7-8', and the reporter pages could not be confirmed.
what_it_supports: Nothing. The load-bearing clause is the second branch, which needs no support from Ames.
what_it_does_not_establish: That P3 is fatal. It is one clause in a disjunctive whose other branch carries the weight.
notes: THE SURGICAL FIX. Delete the words 'fall within the carveouts recognized in Ames or' from P3 and let the sentence read '...the pleaded theories attack the enforceability of the underlying obligation independent of any assignment.' That is accurate, it is what the counts do, and it removes the only sentence in the pleading an opponent could use to argue the drafter misread the controlling case.
